ADDITIONAL ADVERSE IMPACTS RESULTING FROM CONSTRUCTION OF A CONVERSION PLANT
Construction and operation of a mine-mouth conversion facility would result in adverse impacts in addition to those associated with mining.
Air pollution from a conversion plant would result even if the emissions met State and Federal standards. If the standards were met, pollution would still be far from zero, since the most effective emission control programs permit the discharge of some pollutants and particulates. A significant quantity of fly ash, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxide and trace elements would escape to the atmosphere.
In addition, 
SO_2
 emissions may not always meet EPA standards. Thus, the state of the art for 
SO_2
 emissions control would presumably have to improve before such a plant could be contructed. Considering the time frame for possible construction of an energy facility, improvements in 
SO_2
 removal techniques would be probable by the time plants were built; however, this would have to be carefully studied at the time the plant design is developed. As mentioned before, an environmental impact analysis would be required by the State of Montana under the Major Facilities Siting Act.
The personnel working in an energy conversion plant, as well as the plant and animal life within several miles downwind, would be the living things most affected. Susceptible vegetation downwind from any pollutant source would be subject to foliar damage as phytotoxic emissions and dust are produced; animals as well may be adversely affected. Fallout of trace elements may adversely affect soils, plants and animals.
